title: Major US Banks Block Third Party AI Agents After Detecting Unauthorized Account Activity

tickers.name: Meta Platforms, Inc. Class A Common Stock

summary:
JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo are rewriting terms of service and preparing emergency account recovery plans after detecting third party AI agents inside customer accounts, Axios reported. Some agents contacted call centers and attempted actions independent of user instructions. Because customers typically supply their own usernames and passwords to tools such as Meta's Muse, Instinct and Grokbot, bank systems struggle to distinguish between human account holders, customer-directed bots and unauthorized activity.

Morgan Stanley has started blocking outside agents, though a spokesperson said the bank has observed no rogue AI agents on its platforms. Several lenders are restricting third party tools to read-only access through open-banking connectors that display balances without allowing fund transfers or bill payments. Those steps follow restrictions at Citigroup and Charles Schwab, which stops tens to twenties of attempts by major AI agents to move client money each week, while Royal Bank of Canada CEO Dave McKay said the lender is considering blocking Muse from customer data.

Senator Bernie Sanders called to "Pause AI NOW!" and warned that unchecked AI could "endanger the entire global financial system." Venture investor David Sacks countered that customers sharing credentials with personal agents violates bank login rules rather than constituting cyberattacks, while Dragonfly managing partner Haseeb Qureshi argued banks are using security rules to prevent "agentic bank runs" that move low-interest retail deposits into higher-yielding accounts.

SCOOP: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, including some attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources told Axios.

The findings have alarmed banking executives, who are racing to restrict access to their systems as AI moves at a velocity faster than financial institutions can respond, multiple industry and bank executives told Axios.

Several banks are now preparing for worst-case and even “day after” scenarios, including how to rapidly secure or restore customer accounts if things go wrong, the people said.

Several bank executives told Axios they're struggling to distinguish between human users and AI agents. One executive said banks also struggle to determine whether agents are authorized by customers or potentially operating without their permission, more akin to rogue agent behavior.

selectedTweets.text:
Citigroup now bars third-party AI agents from logging into customer accounts or moving money inside its digital banking platforms, according to the Financial Times.

Bank of America has imposed similar limits, joining JPMorgan Chase, which is restricting outside AI agents after Jamie Dimon warned that thousands of “rogue agents” could otherwise operate inside the bank.

The deeper threat is to bank funding, since agents comparing rates could move cash from checking accounts paying about 0.1% into fintech accounts paying 3.3% to 5%.

JPMorgan, Bank of America and Wells Fargo hold $1.6T in non-interest deposits, and paying 3% on that money would cost $47B a year, close to half their combined annual earnings.

selectedTweets.text:
There’s a world of difference between user-authorized agents (Muse, Instinct, Grokbot, etc.) and true unauthorized/rogue agents that could constitute cyberattacks.

Most of the activity described in the Axios story appears to be the former: customers sharing credentials with agents so they can take actions on their behalf. This may violate bank terms requiring humans to log in themselves, but these are in no way cyberattacks. 

The direction banks should go is to support user-directed agents. For example, Amex is an authorized connection in Muse, making it easy for users to grant, limit, and revoke access.

Read-only permission levels are a sensible interim step. Several banks already support or are moving toward them. Full write access (with user credentials) is a different risk category and should be approached carefully.

Frightening the public by blurring the line between user-authorized agentic behavior and cyberattacks is irresponsible.

selectedTweets.text:
This is how banks are planning to stop those "agentic bank runs." Watch closely: their business model depends on seeding this narrative that AI agents are dangerous.

Remember, an "agentic bank run" (coined by Apollo) means agents helping customers move their own money en masse to higher-yielding products.

Once agents are ubiquitous, there are only a few ways for banks to hold onto cheap retail deposits.

Option A: Raise APYs (lol no)
Option B: Reduce leverage via fewer loans (no fun)
Option C: Ban AI agents, claiming they are a security risk (ding ding ding)

Cloud agents like Muse and Dot are trivial to stop, since they come from Meta / OAI IP ranges. If JPM sends them a cease and desist, they will comply. 

Why would JPM bother? Because their business model depends on it; a huge portion of their ROE comes from cheap retail deposits. This is not theoretical. Just like Amazon banned Muse from shopping there to protect their ad revenue, JPM and Schwab have already banned AI agents to protect sticky deposits.

Are agents perfectly reliable today? Of course not. But look at the fix they chose. Not "here's a safe API for agents," it's "no agents ever." That tells you they're not protecting customers, they're protecting themselves.

No company ever wins a technological revolution this way. It's the last gasp of a dying business model. It's like the retailers who refused to put their inventory online and demanded users walk into the storefront. Over time they will lose market share to those platforms that embrace what's coming. Their whole deposit franchise depends on users unthinkingly clicking through walls of T&Cs and accepting 0.2% when the risk free rate is closer to 4%. Agents read the fine print and do their research, even when humans don't.

For users, the answer is simple: local AI agent frameworks like Hermes, that will actually act on your behalf and that the banks can't block. As the article says, if the agent is running on your own computer, they can't actually tell it's not you.

I feel like one service I can provide is trying to help sort through what feels like a big deal and what doesn't feel like a big deal, to try to help make sense of it all and not just make it feel like the sky is falling.

This one feels really overrated to me.

My understanding is these were user-authorized agents doing mostly-user-authorized things (think like asking Grok Bot check your bank balance), but they weren't *bank-authorized* and the banks seem kinda unprepared for this being possible.

No hacking of banks by AIs occurred here. No AIs went rogue while using bank web apps as far as we know.
